Chapter 1: Discovering the Enneagram — A Map for Understanding Ourselves.
Have you ever felt like there’s something about yourself that you just can’t quite put your finger on? Almost as if you’re being nudged along by habits and hopes you don’t even realize are there?
That’s where the Enneagram comes in. For a lot of people, discovering it feels like getting a gentle invitation to look under the hood—to see what’s actually steering the wheel.
Now, maybe you’ve heard about the Enneagram and thought, “Oh, just another personality test.” But here’s the thing: it’s not about sticking you in a box. Far from it. What makes the Enneagram different is that it helps you notice the patterns you’ve been carrying around for years—sometimes without even knowing it.
The Enneagram lays out nine core types, and each type comes with its own unique set of motivations, fears, and ways of seeing the world. It’s not about slapping on a label. It’s about shining a light on the stories you tell yourself—the ones you might’ve started believing long before you could explain them.
Picture a friend who’s always chasing after perfection, never quite happy with how things turn out. Or maybe you know someone who’s always on high alert, scanning for what could go wrong. These aren’t just quirks. They’re deeper patterns, shaped by beliefs about what it takes to feel safe or loved in the world. The Enneagram gives us a way to name these patterns. And with a name comes understanding—not judgment.
One of the first things the Enneagram teaches is this: sure, you have a core type, but that’s just the beginning of the story. You’re way more complex than any single description. Think of the Enneagram as a map, not a cage.
It helps you notice those gut reactions under stress, the things you’re always longing for, and those pesky blind spots you keep tripping over. It’s not about self-improvement in the usual sense—it’s about self-knowledge. Here’s the real goal: not to become a “better” version of your type, but to become more aware, more compassionate, and a little more free.
I’m reminded of someone who, after years of feeling misunderstood, read a description of their type and felt as if someone had been eavesdropping on their inner life. Suddenly, there was a language for all those things they’d never been able to explain. Relief washed over them. But with that relief came a new challenge: to honestly look at how their type had shaped their relationships, their work, even their spiritual life.
Here’s something to keep in mind—the Enneagram doesn’t hand out quick fixes. Instead, it gently asks you to slow down and really pay attention. It poses those tough questions most of us would rather avoid: What are you scared of? What do you truly want? How do you act when you don’t get it?
Most of us spend a lifetime dodging those questions. The Enneagram makes it feel safe to finally ask them. It’s not about shame or blame—it’s about curiosity and kindness.
As you start exploring your type, you’ll probably notice patterns that have always been there. The way criticism stings, the things that make you anxious, those habits that pop up whenever you’re under pressure—they finally make sense.
It’s a bit like switching on the lights in a room that’s been dim for years. Suddenly, you can see the furniture, and you can move around without bumping into things.
But the Enneagram isn’t just about understanding yourself. It’s also about growing in compassion. Once you see your own patterns, it gets a lot easier to realize everyone else has their own invisible battles. Maybe that colleague who seems distant is just trying to avoid disappointment. Or the friend who can never say no? Maybe they’re terrified of being left out.
The Enneagram helps you look past the surface—and respond with empathy instead of snap judgments.
